regime.paragraph: Markets moved without a single dominant theme: US Treasury yields 2Y -6bp to 4.61% and 10Y -7bp to 4.98%. The US curve saw a bull flattener in 2s10s (-1bp to 37bp). The dollar fell 0.2%, gold fell 0.5%, the S&P 500 fell 0.3% and Brent fell 2.6%. US high-yield spreads tightened 4bp. The standout move was USD/CNY (-0.3%, 3.9x its 20-day volatility).

regions.name: United States
regions.text: Treasuries rallied, 2Y -6bp to 4.61% and 10Y -7bp to 4.98%: a bull flattener (2s10s -1bp). Fed pricing was steady at +64bp over 12 months. The dollar fell 0.2% and the S&P 500 fell 0.3%.

regions.name: United Kingdom
regions.text: Gilts sold off with the front end leading, 2Y +3bp to 4.77% and 10Y unch to 5.33%: a bear flattener (2s10s -3bp). Gilts underperformed Treasuries by 7bp at 10Y. BoE pricing was steady at +119bp over 12 months. Sterling rose 0.4% and the FTSE 100 rose 0.3%.

relationships.statement: Lower US yields weighed on the dollar.
relationships.lesson: Higher US yields raise the return on dollar assets and attract capital. When the dollar moves against yields, risk sentiment or non-US news is usually driving FX instead.

relationships.statement: Narrower Treasury–Bund spreads favoured EUR over USD.
relationships.lesson: FX tends to follow relative rates: a wider US–German yield gap raises the carry on USD versus EUR. Front-end (2Y) differentials usually matter more than 10Y.

relationships.statement: Lower oil pulled US breakevens down.
relationships.lesson: Energy feeds directly into headline inflation, so short-dated breakevens track oil closely.
Gold pays no coupon, so higher real yields raise the opportunity cost of holding it. A break often reflects central-bank buying, geopolitical hedging or dollar moves.

relationships.statement: Tighter BTP–Bund spreads signalled stronger demand for periphery risk.
relationships.lesson: BTP–Bund is the euro area's main gauge of sovereign and fragmentation risk; it usually widens with risk-off and narrows when risk appetite is strong.

interview.question: Was today's Treasury rally driven by real yields or inflation expectations?
interview.answer: Nominal yields fell 7.0bp, driven by both real yields and inflation expectations (real +3.0bp, breakeven -3.0bp). Nominal yield = real yield + breakeven inflation. Real-yield-led moves usually reflect policy expectations or growth; breakeven-led moves reflect inflation risk, often energy prices. Brent moved -2.6%.

interview.question: Why did Treasuries outperform Bunds?
interview.answer: 10Y Treasuries moved -7bp versus -1bp for Bunds, so the spread moved -6bp to 156bp (92th percentile of the past year). Cross-market spreads remove the global rates move and isolate local drivers: domestic data surprises, relative central-bank repricing, and supply or fiscal news. Check whether the front end (2Y spread) moved too: if it did, it is a policy story; if only the long end moved, it is term premium.

interview.question: What is the market pricing for the European Central Bank, and what changed today?
interview.answer: Policy rate 2.50%. Markets price a 75% chance of a 25bp hike at the next meeting and 2.6 hikes (64bp) over 12 months; terminal 3.31%. The 12-month pricing moved +5bp on the day. Method: Government bill-curve proxy (indicative). Remember that one 25bp move is 25bp of pricing, so +64bp is 2.6 moves.

interview.question: Why did BTP–Bund spreads tighten?
interview.answer: BTP–Bund moved -4bp to 104bp. The spread prices Italian sovereign credit and redenomination risk relative to Germany. It widens with global risk-off, Italian fiscal or political news, or a hawkish ECB (higher rates raise debt-servicing concerns), and tightens with strong risk appetite and carry demand. The ECB's TPI backstop limits disorderly widening. Today's Euro Stoxx move was +0.6%.

interview.question: Why did the dollar weaken?
interview.answer: DXY moved -0.2% alongside a -7bp move in 10Y Treasuries and -6bp in the US–Germany 2Y spread. The textbook link is relative rates: higher US yields versus the rest of the world raise the carry on USD.
